newsitem.title: JAPAN: Bond giant Nomura takes a hit, but comeback likely.
newsitem.headline: Bond giant Nomura takes a hit, but comeback likely.

text.p: Penalties against Nomura Securities Co Ltd for its role in a payoff scandal may spur investors and bond issuers to take their business elsewhere, but the giant is likely to return to prominence once the penalties expire, bond market sources say.

"Even investors who are still trading (with Nomura) are apparently thinking about reviewing their trading practices ...so I think there is no question that there will be an additional flight of investors (away from Nomura)," said a senior trader for a city bank's securities unit.

Various investors both public and private, including Japan's huge Postal Life Insurance Bureau and Postal Savings Bureau, as well as investment management companies and trust banks, have already suspended business with Nomura, but others stuck with the brokerage even after it became embroiled in scandal.
Nomura exerts a powerful influence on every area of business in the yen bond market and is Japan's top seller of foreign bonds.

On Wednesday, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) said it would suspend Nomura from Japanese government bond (JGB), municipal bond and government-guaranteed bond underwriting syndicates until the end of the year, extending a provisional ban already in effect since May.

The ministry also extended until the year's end a ban on participation in JGB and public bond underwriting by Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB), another leading Japanese financial institution caught up in the scandal.

Nomura's woes have opened a window of opportunity for foreign houses, whose sophisticated hedging technology enables them to trade in large lots with greater ease than many Japanese brokerage houses, market sources said.

"I hear that some investors have found it hard to sell, say, 50 billion yen ($423 million) or 100 billion yen ($847 million) worth of bonds through domestic brokerages other than Nomura, and that such investors are now mainly trading with foreign brokerages," a senior trust bank trader said.

Although Nomura's business may take a hit over the term of its punishment, it is likely to return to its dominant position once the measures are lifted, a senior trader for a foreign brokerage said. In the long-term, many say Nomura will be able to win back investors.

"Nomura has strong sales networks throughout the country, which cover even small investors. Nomura's strength lies in its ability to deal with such small investors on the one hand, while dealing with large investors on the other. This is something that foreign brokerages just cannot compete with," the senior foreign brokerage trader said.

With regard to international bonds, the announcement of punitive measures against Nomura may have little effect overall, due to its strong reputation in the samurai and euroyen markets, underwriters said.
Nomura may lose some market share temporarily, but overseas issuers are not likely to stay away from Nomura in the long term, a senior underwriter at a brokerage house said.
In the primary market for corporate bonds, Nomura's share of bond underwriting has fallen from 14 percent in fiscal 1996 to 3.2 percent so far this year, a bond market analyst said.

The void left by Nomura has so far been filled by Daiwa Securities Co Ltd, Nikko Securities Co Ltd, Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd and bank-affiliated brokerages, but current market shares may change over time.
On Wednesday, prosecutors raided the offices of Yamaichi Securities, which is suspected of giving about 80 million yen ($677,000) to Ryuichi Koike, a corporate racketeer.
Analysts said that the greatest worry Nomura faces is the potential loss of key personnel and talented traders.

"Probably the biggest risk of all is not the lack of short-term trading profits, but the fact that the street is being flooded with Nomura resumes. If you just go to the fax machine there are piles of resumes from people at Nomura," a strategist for a foreign brokerage house said.
"If their key people actually jump to different firms, the long-term impact would be enormous," he said.
